title: Strategic Analysis: External Environment
outcomes: Explain the business environment and apply PESTLE.
Analyse products, industries and life cycles.

meta.exam_tip: Always end a five-forces or PESTLE answer with an overall conclusion about the industry.

concepts.title: Business environment and PESTLE analysis
body: The business environment comprises forces outside the firm that affect its performance: the micro environment (customers, suppliers, competitors, intermediaries, public) and the macro environment (broad forces).
PESTLE examines political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors to spot opportunities and threats.
Environmental analysis must be continuous, because changes in regulation, technology or consumer behaviour can quickly reshape an industry.
concepts.analogy: Scanning the environment is like checking the weather before a voyage.
concepts.work: A change in data-protection law affects every app-based business — a legal factor.

concepts.title: Product, industry and the industry life cycle
body: A product is anything offered to satisfy a need; an industry is a group of firms offering close substitutes. Dominant economic features include market size and growth, number of rivals, scale economies, technology change and capital needs.

Industries and products pass through a life cycle: introduction (low sales, high costs), growth (rising sales, new entrants), maturity (slow growth, intense competition) and decline (falling demand, exits). Strategies differ by stage.
Understanding the market and customers — segments, needs, buying behaviour — is essential for positioning.
concepts.analogy: Where an industry is in its life cycle shapes what strategies make sense.
concepts.work: Landline phones are in decline; EV charging is in growth.

concepts.title: Porter's five forces
body: Porter's five forces explain industry profitability: threat of new entrants (barriers such as scale, capital, brand, regulation), bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of substitutes, and rivalry among existing competitors.
Strong forces squeeze average profits; weak forces allow higher returns. Firms use the analysis to position themselves where forces are weakest or to influence them.
Rivalry is intense when competitors are many and equal, growth is slow, fixed costs are high, products are similar and exit barriers are high.
concepts.analogy: Profitability depends not just on rivals but on five pressures around the industry.
concepts.work: Airlines face strong buyers, powerful suppliers (aircraft makers), substitutes (trains) and fierce rivalry.

concepts.title: Key success factors, strategic groups and competitor analysis
body: Key success factors (KSFs) are the few things a firm must do well to succeed in an industry, such as distribution reach in FMCG or technology in software.
Strategic groups cluster firms that follow similar strategies (price, quality, geographic scope); rivalry is strongest within a group.
Competitor analysis studies rivals' objectives, strategies, strengths and likely moves. Together with KSFs, this helps choose competitive strategy.
concepts.analogy: Know what wins in your industry and who you are really competing with.
concepts.work: Luxury car makers form a strategic group distinct from budget car makers.

illustrations.title: PESTLE for electric two-wheelers
illustrations.q: An Indian company plans to launch electric two-wheelers. Give one factor under each PESTLE head and its likely effect.

head: Head
Factor
Effect
rows: Political
Government push for clean mobility and local manufacturing
Supportive policies and incentives
Economic
Fuel price levels and consumer credit availability
Running-cost savings drive demand; EMIs make purchase easier
Social
Young urban buyers' interest in sustainability and app-based services
Positive acceptance; need for digital features
Technological
Falling battery costs and better charging infrastructure
Lower prices, longer range
Legal
Battery safety standards and vehicle certification rules
Higher compliance cost; safer products
Environmental
Urban air pollution concerns and battery disposal issues
Demand boost; need for recycling plans

illustrations.title: How attractive is the industry?
illustrations.q: Apply Porter's five forces to the Indian quick-commerce grocery delivery industry and conclude on its attractiveness.

head: Force
Assessment
rows: Threat of new entrants
High — well-funded players can enter, though dark-store networks and brand recall create some barriers
Bargaining power of buyers
High — customers switch apps easily and compare prices
Bargaining power of suppliers
Moderate — big brands have power; local suppliers have little
Threat of substitutes
High — neighbourhood stores, supermarkets and e-commerce
Rivalry among existing firms
Intense — heavy discounting and fast expansion
solution.title: Five forces

solution.text: With most forces strong, average profitability is likely to be low unless a firm builds scale, efficiency and loyalty.

jobs.title: Industry note for a lender
jobs.situation: A bank asks for an industry view before lending to a cement maker.
steps: Identify KSFs and the client's strategic group.
jobs.takeaway: Industry structure often explains more about future profits than the firm's own past.

mcqs.q: In PESTLE, a change in consumer lifestyles falls under:
mcqs.explain: Lifestyles, demographics and culture are social factors. In practice: affect product design.

mcqs.q: Which force is weakened by high capital requirements?
mcqs.explain: High capital needs are an entry barrier. In practice: steel and telecom have such barriers.

options: Industry growth is slow and products are similar
mcqs.explain: Slow growth and commoditised products push firms to fight for share. In practice: price wars follow.

options: Switching costs are low and buyers are concentrated
mcqs.explain: Easy switching and big buyers raise bargaining power. In practice: large retailers squeeze suppliers.

mcqs.q: During the maturity stage of the industry life cycle:
mcqs.explain: Maturity brings saturation and share battles. In practice: cost efficiency matters.
mcqs.topic: Product, industry and the industry life cycle

options: Things a firm must do well to succeed in an industry
mcqs.explain: KSFs vary by industry. In practice: distribution, technology or brand.
mcqs.topic: Key success factors, strategic groups and competitor analysis

options: Firms in an industry following similar strategies
mcqs.explain: Mapping strategic groups shows closest rivals. In practice: use price and scope axes.
mcqs.topic: Key success factors, strategic groups and competitor analysis

mcqs.q: The threat of substitutes refers to:
options: Products from other industries meeting the same need
New firms in the same industry
mcqs.explain: Substitutes cap prices. In practice: video calls substitute business travel.

summary: Industry life cycle: introduction, growth, maturity, decline.
Five forces: entrants, buyers, suppliers, substitutes, rivalry.
remember: Strong forces mean lower average profits.
traps: Substitutes come from other industries, not rivals.

viva.model: A tool for scanning the macro environment under political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors.
Threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of substitutes and rivalry among existing competitors.

viva.q: What happens in the growth stage of an industry?
viva.model: Sales rise rapidly, new competitors enter and firms invest in capacity and brand building.
To focus resources on the few capabilities that decide success in the industry.
Economies of scale and high capital requirements, along with brand loyalty and regulation.

cases.title: BrewCraft Coffee
cases.case: BrewCraft runs premium cafés in metro cities. Coffee bean prices are rising due to poor harvests, many new cafés are opening, customers easily switch to rivals or make coffee at home, and the Government is considering higher taxes on packaged beverages.

mcqs.explain: Input scarcity strengthens suppliers. In practice: consider long-term contracts.
It meets the same need from outside the café industry. In practice: limits pricing power.

mcqs.q: Possible higher beverage taxes are a(n):
mcqs.explain: Government policy and law fall under political and legal. In practice: monitor budget announcements.

options: Low entry barriers and rising rivalry
mcqs.explain: Easy entry increases competition. In practice: differentiate through experience.
